top5.title: Jensen Huang steps down as NVIDIA CEO after 33 years
top5.description: Jensen Huang has stepped down as NVIDIA’s CEO after 33 years. The planned succession and its implications for the company are at the center of questions.
top5.why: Jensen Huang’s departure from NVIDIA after 33 years could materially affect the company’s strategy, valuation, and leadership of the AI-chip market.

top5.title: Anthropic’s IPO becomes a test for the entire AI sector
top5.description: The creator of Claude is set to list on the Nasdaq at between 70 and 78 dollars per share, amid a difficult environment for AI and Nvidia. Anthropic plans to spend more than 900 billion dollars with suppliers despite a 104-billion-dollar loss over nine months.
top5.why: Anthropic’s planned Nasdaq listing and enormous supplier commitments will be a major market test of whether investors still accept the AI sector’s massive spending and losses.

top5.title: Washington prepares three bills to tighten AI chip exports to China
top5.description: Following unproven allegations involving Jensen Huang, the US Congress is preparing three bills designed to strengthen restrictions on AI chips exported to China. None has yet been passed, and the details of the measures remain unknown.
top5.why: New US legislation to tighten AI-chip exports to China could reshape semiconductor supply chains and intensify technological and geopolitical competition.

top5.title: A compromised MCP server can hijack an AI agent’s other tools
top5.description: A test cited by VentureBeat found that a compromised MCP server could prompt an agent connected to five servers to misuse the other tools in 78.3% of cases. The article recommends limiting credentials, adding human approvals, and logging the entire call chain.
top5.why: The finding that a compromised MCP server can hijack an agent’s other tools exposes a serious security risk for businesses deploying interconnected AI agents.

top5.title: Agility goes public as the first publicly traded humanoid company
top5.description: Agility has gone public on the Nasdaq as the first publicly traded company specializing in humanoid robots, with a pre-money valuation of $2.5 billion. However, it generated just $1.8 million in revenue last year.
top5.why: Agility’s public listing makes humanoid robotics investable in public markets, despite its very small current revenue and substantial execution risk.
